title: Delaware Court of Chancery M&A Deliberation: Twitter Special Committee & Board Deliberations on Musk Acquisition Offer
context: Verbatim-reconstructed high-stakes corporate board and special committee deliberations drawn from Delaware Court of Chancery trial exhibits (C.A. No. 2022-0613-KSJM) and SEC Schedule 14A proxy disclosures. Captures Twitter Inc.'s Board of Directors evaluating Elon Musk's unsolicited $54.20 per share cash buyout proposal, the adoption of a shareholder rights plan ('poison pill') under Unocal, financial fairness evaluations under Revlon, merger agreement representations regarding fake accounts/mDAU, Delaware Material Adverse Effect (MAE) standards, and specific performance enforcement covenants.

metadata.court_record: Delaware Court of Chancery, C.A. No. 2022-0613-KSJM
metadata.entity: Twitter, Inc. Board of Directors & Transaction Committee

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: Good morning directors and advisors. I call this special meeting of the Twitter Board of Directors to order. As disclosed in the Schedule 13D amendment filed this morning, Mr. Elon Musk has delivered an unsolicited non-binding acquisition proposal to purchase 100 percent of Twitter for $54.20 per share in cash, valuing the enterprise at approximately $44 billion. In his transmission, Mr. Musk declared this is his 'best and final' offer, stated he has no confidence in current management, and warned that if his proposal is not accepted, he would reconsider his position as our largest shareholder holding 9.2 percent of common stock. Today we must assess whether to engage, evaluate standalone valuation, and review defensive mechanisms.

turns.speaker: Parag Agrawal
turns.text: Thank you, Bret. From management's perspective, this offer arrives when our multi-year strategic roadmap is just beginning to deliver results. Under our long-range plan presented at Analyst Day, management projected achieving $7.5 billion in annual revenue and 315 million monetizable daily active users by year-end 2023. At $54.20, the offer represents a 38 percent premium over our pre-announcement close, but it is substantially below our 52-week high of $73.34 and materially undervalues our intrinsic long-term growth potential and platform value. Furthermore, the abrupt threat to dump shares creates market disruption.

turns.speaker: Ned Segal
turns.text: Looking at the macroeconomic headwinds, digital advertising spend is contracting industry-wide due to rising interest rates and post-pandemic ad budget revisions. While management's long-range plan targets are robust, achieving $7.5 billion in revenue requires an aggressive 22 percent compound annual growth rate in an increasingly fragile ad market. Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan have provided preliminary standalone discounted cash flow analyses. We must soberly weigh the execution risks of the standalone plan against an immediate, fully funded cash transaction.

turns.speaker: Michael Voris
turns.text: Goldman Sachs has performed preliminary valuation analyses based on management's standalone projections. Our discounted cash flow valuation yields an implied standalone range of $42.00 to $60.50 per share, using discount rates between 9.5 percent and 11.5 percent and terminal growth rates of 2.5 to 3.5 percent. A selected public company trading multiples analysis yields a range of $36.00 to $51.00 per share. Therefore, Mr. Musk's $54.20 cash offer sits near the midpoint of the standalone DCF range, but significantly above current comparable trading multiples. Crucially, the offer contains zero financing commitments at this hour.

turns.speaker: David Faber
turns.text: J.P. Morgan concurs with Goldman's financial baseline. A key risk factor is that Mr. Musk's letter offers zero details on debt or equity financing. Without committed equity financing or executed debt commitment letters from reputable investment banks, this proposal is effectively an unfunded option. If Mr. Musk continues acquiring shares in the open market, he could accumulate a de facto control block without paying a full control premium to minority shareholders.

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: Directors, as Delaware counsel, I advise that your fiduciary duties under Delaware General Corporation Law are governed initially by the Unocal standard. In evaluating an unsolicited, coercive proposal accompanied by threats of hostile creeping accumulation or market dumping, the Board possesses broad authority to protect corporate franchise integrity. To prevent an unnegotiated creeping acquisition of control without an adequate control premium, the Board should immediately consider adopting a limited-duration shareholder rights plan—a poison pill—with a 15 percent ownership trigger threshold.

turns.speaker: Patrick Pichette
turns.text: As Audit Committee Chair, I support preparing the rights plan. We cannot negotiate with a gun to our head. If Mr. Musk can accumulate 20 or 30 percent in the open market through derivatives or block purchases, the public shareholders lose all bargaining leverage. A 15 percent rights plan forces him to negotiate formally with this board and prove he possesses the $44 billion in capital.

turns.speaker: Martha Lane Fox
turns.text: I agree with Patrick and Martin. Our governance responsibility is to protect all shareholders, not just accommodate a single billionaire's ultimatum. If we institute the rights plan, how long does it remain in effect, and does it legally preclude us from accepting the $54.20 offer if verified financing emerges?

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: The rights plan would expire in exactly one year. Under Delaware law under Unocal and Moran v. Household International, a rights plan does not prevent the Board from accepting an offer; it simply levels the playing field. It incentivizes the bidder to negotiate with the Board rather than wage a coercive tender offer or bypass the Board's Revlon evaluation.

turns.speaker: Egon Durban
turns.text: From a private equity perspective, $54.20 is a very compelling price. If the debt and tech equity markets deteriorate further over the next six months, public shareholders might never see $54.20 again. We should implement the rights plan to preserve our leverage, but we must not shut the door on engaging if he provides fully committed financing letters.

turns.speaker: Robert Zoellick
turns.text: I concur with Egon. The macro geopolitical environment with the war in Ukraine and supply chain disruptions makes technology valuations extremely volatile. A poison pill gives us the necessary defensive shield, but our primary fiduciary duty is maximizing shareholder value, whether standalone or via sale.

turns.speaker: David Rosenblatt
turns.text: Let us authorize the rights plan immediately. Meanwhile, let management and our bankers demand formal proof of financing from Morgan Stanley before we open the data room or commit to substantive merger terms.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: The consensus is clear. Counsel will draft the 15 percent Limited Duration Shareholder Rights Plan for formal board approval tomorrow, while Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan notify Mr. Musk's representatives that the Board requires fully committed debt and equity financing letters.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: Welcome to Round 2 of our deliberations. The Board has formally adopted the shareholder rights plan with a 15 percent trigger. Mr. Musk has responded by filing a definitive Schedule 13D disclosure indicating he has secured $46.5 billion in committed financing, including $25.5 billion in debt and margin loan commitments from Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, and Barclays, alongside a $21.0 billion personal equity commitment letter. He demands an immediate merger agreement by Monday or he will launch a tender offer directly to shareholders.

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: The legal posture has fundamentally shifted. Now that Mr. Musk has delivered fully committed debt and equity financing letters, if the Board determines that pursuing a cash sale of the company is in the best interests of shareholders, our fiduciary duties transition from the defensive Unocal framework to Revlon duties. Under Revlon, Inc. v. MacAndrews & Forbes, your single legal obligation is to obtain the highest transaction value reasonably attainable for the stockholders. There is no other competing bidder in the marketplace.

turns.speaker: Vijaya Gadde
turns.text: In shifting to Revlon, we must examine deal certainty. Mr. Musk's proposed merger agreement is aggressive: he demands the complete elimination of our customary closing conditions, waives all financial and legal due diligence, and insists on signing within 48 hours. If we execute this agreement, we must ensure ironclad contractual protections under Delaware law, specifically Section 9.9 equitable relief and specific performance, to force him to close even if market sentiment sours.

turns.speaker: William Savitt
turns.text: I strongly endorse Vijaya's point. Delaware Court of Chancery precedents like Akorn v. Fresenius and IBP v. Tyson Foods demonstrate that buyers frequently experience buyer's remorse when equity markets drop. In a $44 billion acquisition, we must eliminate any financing contingency, require unconditional regulatory efforts covenants, and stipulate that Twitter can specifically enforce both the merger agreement and the equity commitment letter in Delaware Chancery Court.

turns.speaker: Michael Voris
turns.text: Goldman Sachs has reviewed the financing package. The $13.0 billion senior secured bank debt and $12.5 billion margin loan facility represent binding commitment papers. The $21.0 billion equity commitment is backed by Mr. Musk's liquid holdings and Tesla equity. Financial market sentiment is worsening; the NASDAQ is down 18 percent year-to-date. Finding another bidder capable of offering $44 billion in cash with no regulatory anti-trust barriers is practically zero.

turns.speaker: David Faber
turns.text: J.P. Morgan contacted potential strategic buyers including Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft. As expected, antitrust and regulatory constraints make a strategic acquisition impossible. Private equity sponsors also confirmed that a $44 billion equity check exceeds the syndication capacity of any existing PE consortium. Musk at $54.20 is the only credible transaction in the market.

turns.speaker: Patrick Pichette
turns.text: So under Revlon, this is the highest transaction price reasonably attainable. If we reject $54.20 and the stock collapses back to the mid-$30s, our shareholders will suffer immense capital loss and sue this board. But we cannot sign a loose contract. We need a massive reverse breakup fee and unconditional closing obligations.

turns.speaker: Martha Lane Fox
turns.text: What about company employees and our mission around content moderation and healthy public conversation? Under Revlon, are we permitted to consider platform governance or employee retention, or are we strictly bound by price?

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: In a cash sale where control passes entirely to a private owner, Delaware law is unambiguous: the board cannot trade off stockholder cash value for non-financial stakeholder interests. You are legally required to maximize the cash consideration received by the public stockholders. However, we can negotiate customary employee benefit protections and equity acceleration covenants into the merger agreement.

turns.speaker: Parag Agrawal
turns.text: If we proceed toward an agreement, management will insist on clear operating covenants that allow us to run the business, hire engineers, and maintain platform integrity without micro-management until closing. We must also ensure our public disclosures on spam and monetizable users are protected by standard materiality qualifiers.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: The Board directs our legal counsel Wachtell Lipton and our investment bankers to engage Mr. Musk's counsel, Skadden Arps, to negotiate a definitive merger agreement at $54.20 per share, conditioned on bulletproof deal certainty and Delaware specific performance.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: We are now in Round 3. Counsel and financial advisors have negotiated continuously through the weekend with Mr. Musk's team. Mr. Musk has agreed to the $54.20 cash price without reduction. However, his team has raised objections to our proposed reverse termination fee and our standard representations regarding SEC filings and user data metrics. Let us review the key contractual terms.

turns.speaker: William Savitt
turns.text: We have secured critical victories in the draft merger agreement. First, there is no financing condition of any kind in Section 7.2. Second, Section 9.9 provides Twitter with the explicit right to seek specific performance to compel Mr. Musk to fund his $21 billion equity commitment and consummate the closing. Third, we have agreed upon a $1.0 billion company termination fee if we accept a superior proposal, balanced against a $1.0 billion parent reverse termination fee if Musk fails to close due to debt financing failure.

turns.speaker: Ned Segal
turns.text: Regarding the $1.0 billion reverse termination fee, our bankers and Wachtell must make sure this fee does not function as an option payment allowing Mr. Musk to simply walk away by paying $1.0 billion. In Delaware, a buyer must not be permitted to treat a reverse termination fee as an exclusive cap on liability if they willfully breach the agreement.

turns.speaker: William Savitt
turns.text: Ned is correct. We have drafted Section 8.3 and Section 9.9 such that the $1.0 billion reverse fee is payable solely if the debt financing fails through no fault of Musk. In the event of a willful or material breach by the buyer, our right to specific performance to compel closing remains absolute, and damages are not capped by the termination fee.

turns.speaker: Elon Musk
turns.text: My team at Skadden and Morgan Stanley has made our terms clear. I have waived all standard confirmatory due diligence to move quickly. I am paying an extraordinary $54.20 price when the market is crashing. In exchange, I require Twitter to warrant the accuracy of its financial and operating metrics, particularly regarding fake accounts and spam bots. Twitter's SEC filings claim less than 5 percent of daily active users are false or spam accounts. I am relying on the integrity of those representations.

turns.speaker: Vijaya Gadde
turns.text: Our representations regarding our SEC filings in Section 4.6 and Section 4.7 are carefully circumscribed by our public disclosures. As stated in our 10-K and 10-Q filings, our estimate that false or spam accounts represent fewer than 5 percent of mDAU involves significant judgment, relies on internal sampling methodologies, and may not reflect the actual number of spam accounts across the entire platform. Mr. Musk is expressly put on notice by our public disclosures and cannot claim fraud or breach based on generalized spam estimates.

turns.speaker: David Rosenblatt
turns.text: Musk waived due diligence precisely because he wanted to close quickly without giving us time to shop the company. If he later tries to manufacture a dispute around spam bots to renegotiate the price, does Delaware Chancery Court permit him to escape the contract?

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: Absolutely not. In Delaware, when a sophisticated buyer explicitly disclaims reliance on extra-contractual representations and waives due diligence, they are strictly bound by the four corners of the agreement under Chancellor McCormick's established jurisprudence. To terminate for a breach of representations, the buyer must prove a Material Adverse Effect under Akorn, which requires a catastrophic, company-specific decline that threatens the long-term earnings potential over a commercially reasonable period of years.

turns.speaker: Patrick Pichette
turns.text: This confirms our legal fortress. With specific performance, no financing contingency, and a standard Delaware Material Adverse Effect clause that explicitly excludes general market-wide declines, the deal structure is sound.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: Let us finalize the agreement terms with Skadden Arps and proceed to final financial fairness reviews.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: We convene Round 4. Several weeks have passed since signing the merger agreement on April 25, 2022. As the broader technology sector has endured a severe selloff, Mr. Musk has begun posting public tweets claiming the transaction is 'on hold' pending verification that spam bots represent less than 5 percent of users. He has sent multiple formal letters demanding raw firehose access and accusing Twitter of material breach. We must review our response and prepare for Delaware litigation.

turns.speaker: Parag Agrawal
turns.text: Mr. Musk's public attacks on Twitter's executive team and our spam metrics are damaging employee morale and advertiser relationships. We have provided him with extensive data, including our 30-day historical 'firehose' of more than 500 million daily tweets, our full API documentation, and details of our human review sampling process. Yet he continues to assert in public that 20 percent or more of mDAU are fake, using crude third-party scraping tools that have no access to private IP and phone verification data.

turns.speaker: Elon Musk
turns.text: Twitter has actively obstructed my legal rights under Section 6.4 of the merger agreement to evaluate information reasonably related to consummating the financing. My data science team conducted independent analysis indicating that bot accounts exceed 20 percent. Twitter's repeated refusal to provide core sampling methodologies and raw user logs constitutes a material breach of the information access covenants, discharging my obligation to close.

turns.speaker: Vijaya Gadde
turns.text: That argument is legally frivolous. Section 6.4 only requires Twitter to provide reasonable access to information for 'reasonable business purposes related to the consummation of the transactions.' It is not a license for a buyer to conduct fishing expeditions or perform confirmatory diligence that was explicitly waived before signing. Despite this, we have provided him petabytes of firehose data in good faith.

turns.speaker: William Savitt
turns.text: This is textbook buyer's remorse. Tesla's stock price has declined by over 35 percent since April, which severely impairs the value of Musk's margin loan facility and personal wealth. Having agreed to pay $54.20 at the top of the market, Mr. Musk is manufacturing pretextual claims to renegotiate a price cut or exit the transaction. Under Delaware law, buyer's remorse is not a defense to specific performance.

turns.speaker: Martin Lipton
turns.text: Under Delaware Chancery law, the bar for establishing a Material Adverse Effect is extraordinarily high. In the history of Delaware corporate jurisprudence, only one single case—Akorn v. Fresenius—has ever found an MAE, and that involved massive regulatory fraud and a 50 percent collapse in operating EBITDA. Macroeconomic declines, tech market valuation crashes, and disputes over sample methodologies are expressly excluded from the MAE definition in Section 1.1 of our merger agreement.

turns.speaker: Ned Segal
turns.text: Our Q2 financial results remain stable despite macro headwinds. Revenue grew to $1.18 billion, and average mDAU reached 237.8 million, up 16.6 percent year-over-year. There is zero factual basis for an MAE under Delaware law. We must prepare to file a complaint for specific performance in Delaware Chancery Court the moment he purports to terminate.

turns.speaker: Egon Durban
turns.text: If Musk purports to terminate, we must not hesitate for one second. The Delaware Court of Chancery moves with incredible speed in busted merger disputes. Chancellor Kathaleen McCormick has a proven reputation for enforcing merger agreements strictly according to their plain text.

turns.speaker: Martha Lane Fox
turns.text: I fully support immediate litigation if he breaches. Allowing him to drag our brand through the mud while walking away destroys billions of dollars of shareholder equity. We must demand full compliance with the $54.20 contract.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: The Board confirms our resolute determination. If Mr. Musk issues a notice of termination, Twitter will immediately file suit in Delaware Chancery Court seeking specific performance to compel the closing of the merger at $54.20 per share.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: We convene Round 5. Mr. Musk sent a formal notice purporting to terminate the merger agreement on July 8. Twitter immediately filed suit in Delaware Court of Chancery for specific performance. Trial before Chancellor McCormick was scheduled for October. Seeing that Delaware law would compel him to close, Mr. Musk has folded: his counsel has delivered a letter offering to consummate the merger at the original contract price of $54.20 per share in cash, exactly as agreed on April 25. We are here to reaffirm our unanimous board recommendation and authorize final closing.

turns.speaker: William Savitt
turns.text: Our litigation strategy was completely vindicated. Chancellor McCormick's pre-trial discovery rulings made clear that Delaware enforces merger agreements as written. Faced with the certainty of a decree of specific performance following trial, Mr. Musk abandoned his pretextual claims of bot fraud and MAE. By holding the line, the Board has preserved $44 billion in cash value for our stockholders.

turns.speaker: Michael Voris
turns.text: Goldman Sachs has delivered its final written fairness opinion. In the intervening six months, comparable social media and tech stocks have declined by an average of 45 to 60 percent. Snap is down 75 percent, Meta is down 55 percent. The $54.20 cash price now represents an astonishing 80 to 90 percent premium over where Twitter would trade on a standalone basis today. From a financial perspective, this outcome is historic.

turns.speaker: David Faber
turns.text: J.P. Morgan confirms that the transaction is fully fair, from a financial point of view, to all holders of Twitter common stock. Debt financing is lined up, equity funds are being deposited into escrow, and closing will take place immediately upon resolution of the Delaware proceeding.

turns.speaker: Ned Segal
turns.text: All banking facilities, settlement mechanics, and shareholder disbursement flows through Computershare have been audited and verified. Upon closing, each public share of common stock will be converted into the right to receive $54.20 in cash without interest.

turns.speaker: Patrick Pichette
turns.text: This resolution represents an extraordinary vindication of independent corporate governance and fiduciary duty under Delaware law. The Board protected our shareholders against unprecedented coercion, upheld the integrity of the contract, and secured full value.

turns.speaker: Martha Lane Fox
turns.text: I vote to adopt the resolution and recommend closing. The Board served its true purpose: guarding the financial interests of hundreds of thousands of institutional and retail shareholders.

turns.speaker: Robert Zoellick
turns.text: I vote aye. We demonstrated that rule of law and Delaware contract enforcement govern corporate transactions, regardless of the wealth or celebrity of the acquirer.

turns.speaker: David Rosenblatt
turns.text: I vote aye. The transaction secures full liquidity for our shareholders at a premium that cannot be replicated in the public markets.

turns.speaker: Egon Durban
turns.text: I vote aye. A landmark victory for shareholder value and Delaware corporate law.

turns.speaker: Parag Agrawal
turns.text: I vote aye. Management is proud to have defended the company, protected our people, and brought this transaction to full, definitive completion at $54.20.

turns.speaker: Bret Taylor
turns.text: The resolution is adopted unanimously. The Twitter Board of Directors hereby resolves to approve the consummation of the merger with Mr. Musk's acquisition vehicle at $54.20 per share in cash, authorizes executive officers to execute the closing documents, and directs litigation counsel to file the stipulation of dismissal in Delaware Court of Chancery upon receipt of funds. This meeting is adjourned.
